pages.name: Still there?
pages.task: A coil has an inductance of 0.2 H. What is its reactance on DC, at 0 Hz?
pages.why: X_L = 2π × 0 × 0.2 = 0 Ω. A coil pushes back only while its current changes. On DC the winding's resistance alone sets a steady current. That current sets up a steady flux. How much flux it buys comes next.
pages.alt: An iron ring with a 200-turn coil, carrying 0.1 A. 7 of its 48 small magnets are in line, and the dot sits on the steep part of its curve. Below, the iron's curve of flux density against push rises steeply, bends round a knee at 255 A/m and runs nearly flat. Air's line lies along the bottom.

pages.name: Iron or air
pages.text: 200 turns carrying 0.1 A push 20 At round the ring. The flux is that push divided by the ring's reluctance. In air that buys 0.063 mT. In iron it buys 0.31 T, nearly 5000 times as much.
pages.alt: An iron ring with a 200-turn coil, carrying 0.1 A. 7 of its 48 small magnets are in line, and the dot sits on the steep part of its curve. Below, the iron's curve of flux density against push rises steeply, bends round a knee at 255 A/m and runs nearly flat. Air's line lies along the bottom.

pages.name: Double the current
pages.task: The dot sits at 1 A, reading 1.54 T. You double the current to 2 A. What does the flux density do?
pages.why: At 1 A the curve has already bent over and runs nearly flat. Doubling the current buys only 0.06 T more, from 1.54 T to 1.60 T. Twice the current gives just 4% more flux density.
pages.alt: An iron ring with a 200-turn coil, carrying 2 A. 45 of its 48 small magnets are in line, and the dot sits on the nearly flat part of its curve. Below, the iron's curve of flux density against push rises steeply, bends round a knee at 255 A/m and runs nearly flat. Air's line lies along the bottom.

pages.name: The knee
pages.text: The dot climbs the iron's curve steeply, bends round a knee near 0.5 A and runs nearly flat. At 0.5 A it reads 1.21 T. At 2 A it reads only 1.60 T, with nearly every arrow in the iron in line.
pages.alt: An iron ring with a 200-turn coil, carrying 2 A. 45 of its 48 small magnets are in line, and the dot sits on the nearly flat part of its curve. Below, the iron's curve of flux density against push rises steeply, bends round a knee at 255 A/m and runs nearly flat. Air's line lies along the bottom.

pages.name: Five thousand times
pages.task: In air, 10 ampere-turns on this ring give 0.0314 mT. Take iron as 5000 times air on the steep part of its curve. What flux density does the iron ring reach?
pages.why: 0.0314 mT × 5000 = 157 mT, which is 0.157 T. Iron's reluctance is that much lower. So the same push buys that much more. The drawn curve reads 0.16 T here, as it has barely begun to bend.
pages.alt: An iron ring with a 200-turn coil, carrying 0.05 A. 2 of its 48 small magnets are in line, and the dot sits on the steep part of its curve. Below, the iron's curve of flux density against push rises steeply, bends round a knee at 255 A/m and runs nearly flat. Air's line lies along the bottom.

pages.name: A gap
pages.text: With a 0.25 mm gap, the curve leans over. At 0.5 A the ring reaches 0.38 T, not 1.21 T. At 1 A it reaches 0.75 T, about twice as much.
pages.alt: An iron ring with a 200-turn coil and a 0.25 mm gap, carrying 1 A. 21 of its 48 small magnets are in line, and the dot sits on the nearly flat part of its curve. Below, the iron's curve of flux density against push rises steeply, bends round a knee at 255 A/m and runs nearly flat. Air's line lies along the bottom.

pages.name: Half a millimetre
pages.task: A 0.5 mm gap carries 1.2 T. How many ampere-turns does the gap alone take?
pages.why: 1.2 × 0.0005 ÷ (4π × 10⁻⁷) = 477 At. The iron at 1.2 T needs about 100 At. So half a millimetre of air takes nearly five times the push of the whole iron ring.
pages.alt: An iron ring with a 0.5 mm gap opposite its 200-turn coil. The gap carries 1.2 T. 34 of its 48 small magnets are in line.

pages.name: Round a loop
pages.text: On AC the dot runs round a loop, not up and down one line. At zero current the core keeps a residual flux density of 0.37 T. The loop's shaded area sets the heat left in the iron each cycle.
pages.alt: An iron ring with a 200-turn coil, on AC. 9 of its 48 small magnets are in line. Beside it, on AC, the dot runs round a shaded loop of flux density against push, with the residual flux density marked where the current is zero.

pages.name: Wide or thin
pages.task: Two equal cores of different irons reach the same peak flux density on AC. Iron A's loop is wide. Iron B's loop is thin. Which heats up less each cycle?
pages.why: Each cycle costs heat, set by the loop's area. Both loops are the same height. Iron B's loop is thinner, so it encloses less area. So a core wants an iron with a thin loop.
pages.alt: Two irons' loops of flux density against push, side by side, the same height. Iron A's loop is wide and Iron B's is thin. Their areas are shaded, and Iron B's is the smaller.
options: Neither: they reach the same peak

pages.name: Thinner sheets
pages.task: A core's eddy loss is 40 W. It is rebuilt from sheets half as thick. What is its eddy loss now?
pages.why: Eddy loss goes as the sheet's thickness squared. Half the thickness gives ½ × ½ = ¼ of the loss. So 40 W × ¼ = 10 W. The hysteresis loss does not change, because the loop is the same.

pages.name: Find the knee
pages.task: This ring's knee is at H = 255 A/m. Its path is 0.4 m and its coil has 200 turns. What current puts it at the knee?
pages.why: At the knee the ring needs 255 × 0.4 = 102 At. Shared over 200 turns, that is 0.51 A. Beyond about half an amp, this ring buys less and less flux for each extra amp.
pages.alt: An iron ring with a 200-turn coil, carrying 0.51 A. 35 of its 48 small magnets are in line, and the dot sits round the knee of its curve. Below, the iron's curve of flux density against push rises steeply, bends round a knee at 255 A/m and runs nearly flat. Air's line lies along the bottom.

pages.name: At zero current
pages.task: AC has swung the iron ring round its loop. The current now falls from its peak to zero. What is left in the core?
pages.answer: Some flux, held by the iron
pages.why: Coming down from the peak, the dot does not retrace its climb. Some regions stay in line. So at zero current the core keeps a residual flux density, 0.37 T on this sketch.
pages.alt: An iron ring with a 200-turn coil, on AC. 9 of its 48 small magnets are in line. Beside it, on AC, the dot has come down from the top of the swing to zero current, and the residual flux density is marked.
options: No flux: no current, no field
Some flux, held by the iron
